selected.title: He Secretly Recorded Our Arguments for Months
selected.hook: My boyfriend played our therapist an argument I never knew he'd recorded.
selected.voiceover:
My boyfriend played our therapist an argument I never knew he'd recorded.

We started couples counseling because our fights kept repeating: I said he shut down, he said I exaggerated what happened.

During our third session, the therapist asked for an example.

He pulled out his phone and said, "Actually, I have one."

Then my voice started playing.

It was an argument from our kitchen two weeks earlier. I recognized it instantly. What I didn't recognize was the recording.

I asked when he started doing this.

He admitted it wasn't the first time.

For months, he'd been recording pieces of our arguments whenever he thought I was being "unfair." He had folders labeled by date, notes, even timestamps for moments he wanted to bring up later.

He said it wasn't spying because he was in the conversations too.

But I'd spent months believing our worst moments ended when the fight ended. Apparently, he was building an archive.

The therapist stopped the recording and asked why he felt he needed evidence instead of trust.

Afterward, he said the recordings proved he wasn't imagining things and offered to delete them if I "really cared that much."

That made it worse.

I wasn't upset because the clips made me look bad.

I was upset because every argument had secretly become something he could save and replay.

Would you see that as protecting yourself, or as a relationship boundary you couldn't come back from?

A couples-therapy session took an unexpected turn when her boyfriend played an argument she never knew had been recorded. Then she learned it wasn't the only one. Is keeping private recordings of relationship fights a way to protect your memory, or a breach of trust that changes every conversation afterward?
